newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke may hold rates until polls - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke may hold rates until polls - analysts.

text.p: A fall in British inflation in December, coupled with the soaring pound and evidence of slow pre-Christmas sales may give the government enough ammunition to keep interest rates on hold until the election, economists said on Friday.

But December retail sales and fourth-quarter gross domestic product data due in the next two weeks will be crucial and any sign of above-trend growth might yet coax Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise rates in February, they said.

"There is a good chance that the next tightening in monetary policy will occur as soon as (the February 5 monetary meeting), but we are far from confident that this will happen," said Union Plc chief economist Philip Shaw.
Ian Stewart from Merrill Lynch agreed that it was a difficult decision to call, while adding: "I think on balance the Chancellor probably won't raise rates before the election.

"But you've got to be careful with Clarke. He surprised the market in October when he raised rates and another 25 basis point rise won't make a great difference to the Convervatives' election chances."

Both headline and underlying inflation slipped in December, to 2.5 percent and 3.1 percent, respectively. This was seen to justify Clarke's decision on Wednesday to keep interest rates on hold at 6.0 percent.
The uncertainty surrounding the timing of the next interest rate rise is partly because economic factors are more than usually clouded by political considerations.
"If it was not for this unfortunate conjuncture of the economic and political cycles, rates would be going up," said Stewart.

Several factors make monetary policy unusually difficult to read at the moment -- the election, which must be held by May 22, the impact on consumption of billions of pounds of "windfall" gains from building society mergers and flotations and a dramatic rise in sterling.
"It'll be clearer at the end of next week when we've had the CBI quarterly survey (on Tuesday) and the December retail sales data (on Wednesday)," said Salomon Brothers economist Michael Saunders.
"If those are both weak, it is possible the odds will be in favour of unchanged rates."

But strong fourth quarter GDP data the following week might nudge expectations back again, he added. Evidence of economic growth clearly above the trend rate of around 2.5 percent would sound inflation alarm bells for the Bank of England.

"Were GDP growth in Q4 to be significantly stronger than the 0.6 percent (quarterly rate) considered to be at trend, a refusal by Clarke to raise rates would incur the very public wrath of the Bank of England," said Union's Shaw.
With the economy the central theme of the government's re-election campaign, Clarke will be keen to avoid a public showdown on inflation, he added.
According to a Reuter poll, economists expect GDP to grow by an annual rate of 2.8 percent in the fourth quarter, up from 2.4 percent in the third quarter.
December retail sales are seen rising 0.3 percent on the month giving a 3.8 percent annual rate, down from November's 3.9 percent.
The Conservative Party is some 20 points behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls, so Clarke has a strong political incentive not to raise rates ahead of the election.
"We're a maximum of three months away from an election. So there will be strong political pressure not to move," said Stewart.

The sudden death of a Conservative member of parliament on Thursday, which pushed the government into a minority, could bring the election date forward to the end of March, according to newspaper reports on Friday.
Economists said this would add to the temptation to keep rates on hold.
